pos: n. phrase (Israel's encounter with God at the mountain — the fire, the voice and the terror — and Hebrews' contrast of it with the mountain believers have come to)
etymology: Hebrew Sinay, the mountain of the giving of the Law, also called Horeb. The phrase is modern; the thing it names is the Bible's own standard for what it is like to meet God without a Mediator.
biblical_def: The Sinai experience is the meeting God appointed and the people could not bear. “There were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that was in the camp trembled… and mount Sinai was altogether on a smoke” (Exo 19:16–18). They asked for distance: “let not God speak with us, lest we die” (Exo 20:19). What they received was a voice and no form: “ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice” (Deu 4:12). Hebrews sets a second mountain against it: “ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire… But ye are come unto mount Sion” (Heb 12:18–22), and then refuses to let the contrast go soft: “our God is a consuming fire” (Heb 12:29).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines theophany as a manifestation of God to man by actual appearance; and awe as fear mingled with admiration or reverence, reverential fear — the dread felt in the presence of a superior being.
webster_full: THEOPHANY, n. A manifestation of God to man by actual appearance.
AWE, n. Fear mingled with admiration or reverence; reverential fear.
Stand in awe, and sin not. Ps. 4.
2. Fear; dread inspired by something great, or terrific.
TERROR, n. Extreme fear; violent dread; fright; fear that agitates the body and mind.
scriptures: And it came to pass on the third day in the morning, that there were thunders and lightnings, and a thick cloud upon the mount, and the voice of the trumpet exceeding loud; so that all the people that was in the camp trembled.
And they said unto Moses, Speak thou with us, and we will hear: but let not God speak with us, lest we die.
Deu 4:12
And the LORD spake unto you out of the midst of the fire: ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude; only ye heard a voice.
For ye are not come unto the mount that might be touched, and that burned with fire, nor unto blackness, and darkness, and tempest,
For our God is a consuming fire.
corruption_summary: Sinai is remembered as a spectacle to be sought or a terror to be outgrown, and Hebrews says believers have come to something more solemn, not less.
corruption_paragraphs: The first misuse treats Sinai as the template for meeting God — fire, noise, trembling — and measures every later encounter against it, so that a quiet conversion or an ordinary Lord's day feels like a lesser thing. Exodus itself corrects this. The people who got the spectacle asked for it to stop, and Deuteronomy 4:12 records what they were actually given: a voice, and no similitude. The permanent deposit of Sinai was not the fire but the words, ten of them, written and kept. God's chosen medium at the most theatrical moment in the Old Testament was speech.

The opposite misuse reads Hebrews 12 as Sinai's cancellation: that was law and terror, this is grace and warmth, and the fear is a stage the church has left. But the passage argues from the lesser to the greater, and its logic runs the other way. If they escaped not who refused him that spake on earth, much more shall not we escape if we turn away from him that speaketh from heaven. The believer has come to Sion, to the church of the firstborn, to Jesus the mediator — and the chapter's last word on it is that our God is a consuming fire. Grace is not the removal of the fire but a Mediator standing between it and us.

What Sinai establishes for good is that a sinner cannot meet God directly and live, and that this is not God's cruelty but a fact about holiness in the presence of what is not holy. The people's request in Exodus 20:19 — speak thou with us, and we will hear — is the first cry for a mediator in Scripture, and God's answer in Deuteronomy 18 is that they have well spoken and a Prophet like Moses will be raised up. The whole shape of the gospel is in that exchange: terror at the mountain, a plea for someone to stand between, and a promise that someone will.
roots_summary: Hebrew Sinay (H5514), Sinai; Choreb (H2722), Horeb; qolot (H6963), thunders, voices; Greek pur katanaliskon (G4442, G2654), a consuming fire.
roots_lines: Hebrew qolot (H6963) — thunders, literally voices; Exodus 19:16, 20:18 — the same word as the voice they heard.
Hebrew temunah (H8544) — similitude, form; Deuteronomy 4:12, 4:15–16, Numbers 12:8.
Greek pur katanaliskon (G2654) — consuming fire; Hebrews 12:29, quoting Deuteronomy 4:24.
usage: “Let not God speak with us, lest we die” — the first cry for a mediator.
“Ye heard the voice of the words, but saw no similitude” — the deposit was speech.
“But ye are come unto mount Sion… our God is a consuming fire” — both, in one chapter.

pos: n. phrase (the believer under orders; Paul's figure for a life of discipline, hardship and single loyalty)
etymology: Latin solidus, the coin a Roman soldier was paid in — a soldier is literally a man on a wage, bound by that wage to one commander. Paul uses the figure of Timothy, of Epaphroditus and Archippus, and of himself.
biblical_def: The soldier of Christ is Paul's picture of a disciplined believer: “Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ. No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier” (2Ti 2:3–4). The fight is named: “Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life” (1Ti 6:12). The weapons are not the world's: “the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds” (2Co 10:4). The enemy is not human: “we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers” (Eph 6:12). And the rank is shared: Epaphroditus is “my brother, and companion in labour, and fellowsoldier” (Php 2:25).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines soldier as a man engaged in military service; one whose occupation is military; and, emphatically, a brave warrior, a man of military experience and skill, or a man of distinguished valor.
webster_full: SOLDIER, n. A man engaged in military service; one whose occupation is military; a man enlisted for service in an army; a private, or one in the ranks.
2. A man enrolled for service, when on duty or embodied for military discipline.
3. Emphatically, a brave warrior; a man of military experience and skill, or a man of distinguished valor.
WARFARE, n. Military service; military life; contest carried on by enemies; hostilities; war.
2. Contest; struggle with spiritual enemies.
scriptures: Thou therefore endure hardness, as a good soldier of Jesus Christ.
No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier.
Fight the good fight of faith, lay hold on eternal life, whereunto thou art also called, and hast professed a good profession before many witnesses.
(For the weapons of our warfare are not carnal, but mighty through God to the pulling down of strong holds;)
Eph 6:12
For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places.
corruption_summary: The figure is either dropped as too martial or used to license combat against people, and Paul specifies the enemy, the weapons and the only entanglement that disqualifies.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 6:12 is the clause that governs the whole figure and the church forgets it in both directions. We wrestle not against flesh and blood. A Christian who has turned the language of warfare on his neighbours, his political opponents or the congregation across town has misidentified the enemy, and a militancy aimed at people is not the soldiering Paul describes; it is a desertion to the wrong front. Second Corinthians 10:4 closes the other door — the weapons are not carnal — so the strongholds are pulled down by truth, prayer and the word, not by any force the world would recognise as force.

The embarrassed reaction is the newer error: a church that finds the whole vocabulary distasteful and quietly retires it, leaving believers with no category for the fact that they are opposed. But the figure is Paul's, and he uses it of the gentlest man in his circle. Epaphroditus is a fellowsoldier, and what he did was carry a gift from Philippi and nearly die of illness doing it. Soldiering in the New Testament is mostly endurance, and 2 Timothy 2:3 names exactly that as the duty: endure hardness. The image was chosen for its discipline, not its violence.

Second Timothy 2:4 supplies the single disqualification, and it is not what a moralist expects. No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life — not touches; a soldier eats, sleeps, marries and pays for things. The word is for a net or a snare, the state of being so tied up in ordinary commitments that one cannot move when the order comes. The test is availability. Paul's reason is worth keeping in view too: that he may please him who hath chosen him. The soldier was chosen; he did not enlist himself, and his loyalty answers to that.
roots_summary: Greek stratiotes (G4757), a soldier; strateuomai (G4754), to serve as a soldier, war; emplekomai (G1707), to be entangled, enmeshed; sustratiotes (G4961), a fellowsoldier.
roots_lines: Greek stratiotes (G4757) — soldier; 2 Timothy 2:3, and of the men at the cross, Matthew 27:27.
Greek emplekomai (G1707) — to be entangled, as in a net; 2 Timothy 2:4, 2 Peter 2:20 — both occurrences.
Greek sustratiotes (G4961) — fellowsoldier; Philippians 2:25, Philemon 1:2 — both occurrences.
usage: “Endure hardness, as a good soldier” — the duty named is endurance.
“We wrestle not against flesh and blood” — the enemy, specified.
“Entangleth himself with the affairs of this life” — a net, not a touch.

pos: n. phrase (the song sung on the far side of a rescue — Moses' at the sea, David's in the cave, the redeemed by the glassy sea)
etymology: Hebrew shir, a song, and shirah, its feminine form used of the Song of Moses. The psalms give the genre its name: songs of deliverance, sung by God around the man He has hidden.
biblical_def: The song of deliverance is Israel's first recorded music: “Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD… I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea” (Exo 15:1), and its creed is in the second verse: “The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation” (Exo 15:2). David hears it from outside himself: “Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance” (Psa 32:7). It is given, not composed: “he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD” (Psa 40:3). And the last one joins the first: “they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb” (Rev 15:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines deliverance as release; rescue; the act of delivering from restraint, captivity, slavery or danger; and song as that which is sung, a hymn, a poem to be sung.
webster_full: DELIVERANCE, n. Release from captivity, slavery, oppression, or any restraint.
2. Rescue from danger or any evil.
3. The act of bringing forth children.
SONG, n. In general, that which is sung or uttered with musical modulations of the voice, whether of the human voice or that of a bird.
2. A little poem to be sung, or uttered with musical modulations; a ballad.
3. A hymn; a sacred poem or hymn to be sung either in joy or thanksgiving, as that sung by Moses and the Israelites after escaping the dangers of the Arabian gulf and of Pharaoh's army.
scriptures: Exo 15:1

Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the LORD, and spake, saying, I will sing unto the LORD, for he hath triumphed gloriously: the horse and his rider hath he thrown into the sea.
Exo 15:2
The LORD is my strength and song, and he is become my salvation: he is my God, and I will prepare him an habitation; my father's God, and I will exalt him.
Psa 32:7
Thou art my hiding place; thou shalt preserve me from trouble; thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance. Selah.
Psa 40:3
And he hath put a new song in my mouth, even praise unto our God: many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD.
Rev 15:3
And they sing the song of Moses the servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, Great and marvellous are thy works, Lord God Almighty; just and true are thy ways, thou King of saints.
corruption_summary: The song is treated as a mood available on demand, and Scripture places it after the sea, after the pit, and after the confession.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 15 begins with then — then sang Moses — and the word carries the doctrine. The song comes after the crossing. Israel did not sing on the shore with the army behind them and the water in front; they sang with the water closed and the chariots in it. Scripture's songs of deliverance are retrospective, and their exuberance is earned by a rescue that has actually happened. A church that manufactures the mood without the memory has the music and not the song, and can usually feel the difference.

Psalm 40:3 is careful about authorship: he hath put a new song in my mouth. The verse before it is a pit, miry clay, and feet set upon a rock. The song is placed there by the One who did the lifting, and its effect is stated in the same breath — many shall see it, and fear, and shall trust in the LORD. That is evangelism by biography. Nobody was argued into faith by the singer; they watched a man come out of a pit and heard what he sang about it.

Psalm 32:7 is the strangest of these and the most tender, because David is not the singer. Thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance — God does the singing, around a man who has just spent the first verses of the psalm describing what unconfessed sin did to his bones. The deliverance in that psalm is forgiveness, and the song surrounds the forgiven man like a wall. Revelation 15 closes the canon's music by joining Moses' song to the Lamb's, which is the whole Bible's claim in one duet: the rescue at the sea and the rescue at the cross are one rescue, sung by the same choir.
roots_summary: Hebrew shir / shirah (H7891, H7892), to sing / a song; zimrah (H2176), song, melody — the LORD is my strength and song; ranan (H7442), to shout for joy; Greek ode (G5603), a song.
roots_lines: Hebrew shirah (H7892) — a song; Exodus 15:1, Deuteronomy 31:30, Numbers 21:17, Psalm 18 title.
Hebrew ozzi vezimrath Yah (H5797, H2176) — the LORD is my strength and song; Exodus 15:2, Psalm 118:14, Isaiah 12:2.
Greek ode Moseos…ode tou arniou (G5603) — the song of Moses…the song of the Lamb; Revelation 15:3.
usage: “Then sang Moses” — and then carries the doctrine.
“He hath put a new song in my mouth” — placed there by the One who lifted him.
“Thou shalt compass me about with songs of deliverance” — God singing, around a forgiven man.

pos: n. phrase (the law of the harvest — that a man gathers the kind, and in the proportion, of what he planted)
etymology: Old English sawan and ripan; the figure is agricultural and older than any proverb. Paul's version in Galatians 6 is prefaced by a warning that people are routinely deceived about it.
biblical_def: To sow and reap is the law of the harvest, and Paul states it as something men persistently disbelieve: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap. For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting” (Gal 6:7–8). Hosea gives the proportion: “they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind” (Hos 8:7). The psalm gives the hope: “They that sow in tears shall reap in joy” (Psa 126:5). Paul applies it to giving: “He which soweth sparingly shall reap also sparingly; and he which soweth bountifully shall reap also bountifully” (2Co 9:6). And the interval is named: “in due season we shall reap, if we faint not” (Gal 6:9).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sow as to scatter seed upon the earth for growth; and, figuratively, to spread abroad, to propagate; and reap as to cut grain with a sickle, and, figuratively, to receive as a reward of labor, or as the fruit of works.
webster_full: SOW, v.t. To scatter, as seed upon the earth, for the purpose of growth and the production of a crop.
2. To scatter seed over for growth; as, to sow ground or land.
3. To spread abroad; to propagate; as, to sow discord.
REAP, v.t. To cut grain with a sickle; as, to reap wheat or rye.
2. To gather; to obtain; to receive as a reward, or as the fruit of labor or of works, in a good or bad sense; as, to reap a benefit from exertions.
scriptures: Gal 6:7
Be not deceived; God is not mocked: for whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Gal 6:8
For he that soweth to his flesh shall of the flesh reap corruption; but he that soweth to the Spirit shall of the Spirit reap life everlasting.
Hos 8:7
For they have sown the wind, and they shall reap the whirlwind: it hath no stalk: the bud shall yield no meal: if so be it yield, the strangers shall swallow it up.
They that sow in tears shall reap in joy.
Gal 6:9
And let us not be weary in well doing: for in due season we shall reap, if we faint not.
corruption_summary: The law is made a machine that rules out grace, or waved away by grace so that nothing is reaped; Paul holds both in six verses.
corruption_paragraphs: Galatians 6:7 opens with be not deceived because the deception is the normal state. Nobody argues that seed produces a different crop; what people believe, in practice, is that their own case is an exception — that this particular indulgence will not come up, that this neglect will not be noticed by the soil. Paul's reply is not a threat but a description of how creation works, and he attaches it to God's honour: God is not mocked. A universe in which sowing had no harvest would be one in which God could be fooled.

The harder error for a Reformed reader is to take the law as a complete account of providence, so that every affliction is read as a harvest of some private sowing. Scripture forbids that reading in the book of Job, in the Lord's answer about the man born blind, and in Psalm 73, where the wicked prosper and the psalmist nearly slips. Sowing and reaping is a true law and not the only one; grace interrupts it constantly, and the cross is the place where a Man reaped what He had not sown so that others might reap what they had not either.

Galatians 6:9 supplies the clause that keeps the doctrine from despair, and it is about time. In due season we shall reap — not at once; the interval between seed and harvest is the whole difficulty of farming, and it is also the whole difficulty of faithfulness. Psalm 126:5 puts weeping in the sowing and joy in the reaping, which is the ordinary sequence of ministry, parenthood and prayer, and 2 Corinthians 9:6 adds the proportion: the crop answers to the amount planted. What a man does with that information about his money is not a peripheral application; Paul chose the metaphor for that chapter.
roots_summary: Greek speiro (G4687), to sow; therizo (G2325), to reap; Hebrew zara (H2232), to sow; qatsar (H7114), to reap, harvest.
roots_lines: Greek speiro / therizo (G4687, G2325) — sow / reap; Galatians 6:7–9, 2 Corinthians 9:6, Matthew 13:3–39.
Hebrew zara ruach…suphah (H2232, H7307, H5492) — sown the wind…the whirlwind; Hosea 8:7.
Hebrew hazzore'im bedim'ah (H2232, H1832) — they that sow in tears; Psalm 126:5–6.
usage: “Be not deceived; God is not mocked” — because the deception is the normal state.
“Sown the wind… reap the whirlwind” — the proportion.
“In due season we shall reap, if we faint not” — the interval is the difficulty.

pos: n. phrase (the Holy Spirit as the one who makes the believer's sonship real to him and audible in his prayers)
etymology: Greek pneuma huiothesias — the Spirit of son-placing. Huiothesia is a Roman legal term for the act by which a man not born into a family was made its full heir, and Paul is the only New Testament writer who uses it.
biblical_def: The Spirit of adoption is contrasted with a spirit of slavery: “ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom 8:15). He is sent because of the sonship, not to produce it: “because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father” (Gal 4:6). He testifies inwardly: “The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God” (Rom 8:16). The adoption was decreed: “Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself” (Eph 1:5). And it is not yet complete: “we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body” (Rom 8:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines adoption as the taking and treating of a stranger as one's own child; and, in theology, God's act by which He receives sinful men into His family as sons and heirs, by grace through faith in Christ.
webster_full: ADOPTION, n. The act of adopting, or the state of being adopted; the taking and treating of a stranger as one's own child.
2. The receiving as one's own, what is new or not natural.
3. God's taking the sinful children of men into his favor and protection.
Ye have received the Spirit of adoption. Rom. 8.
ADOPT, v.t. To take a stranger into one's family, as son and heir; to take one who is not a child, and treat him as one, giving him a title to the privileges and rights of a child.
scriptures: Rom 8:15
For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father.
Gal 4:6
And because ye are sons, God hath sent forth the Spirit of his Son into your hearts, crying, Abba, Father.
Rom 8:16
The Spirit itself beareth witness with our spirit, that we are the children of God:
Eph 1:5
Having predestinated us unto the adoption of children by Jesus Christ to himself, according to the good pleasure of his will,
Rom 8:23
And not only they, but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves, waiting for the adoption, to wit, the redemption of our body.
corruption_summary: Assurance is sought in feelings the Spirit is supposed to supply on demand, and Paul locates the witness in a cry the believer is already making.
corruption_paragraphs: Romans 8:15 sets two spirits against each other and the contrast is the diagnosis. The spirit of bondage produces fear; the Spirit of adoption produces a cry. Much religious anxiety is a believer living under the first while possessing the second — approaching God as a slave approaches a master, reckoning his standing by his performance that week, unable to say Father without an apology attached. Paul says that spirit was not what he received. The cure is not a better week but a recognition of which spirit is doing the talking.

Romans 8:16 is the classic text for the Spirit's witness and it is often read as a promise of a private sensation that will settle the question. The verse is more concrete than that. The Spirit beareth witness with our spirit — alongside, jointly — and the immediately preceding clause tells us what the witness sounds like: whereby we cry, Abba, Father. The evidence of adoption is that a man finds himself addressing God as a Father, and cannot stop. Galatians 4:6 adds the order: because ye are sons, God sent the Spirit. The cry does not make the son; it is what a son sounds like.

Romans 8:23 is the clause that keeps the doctrine honest about the present. We are adopted, and we are waiting for the adoption — to wit, the redemption of our body. The legal act is done and the estate is not yet entered upon; meanwhile the heirs groan, and Paul says the whole creation groans with them. A Christian who feels the distance between his standing and his condition is not in doubt about his adoption; he is experiencing exactly what verse 23 says adopted people experience until the body is raised.
roots_summary: Greek huiothesia (G5206), adoption, son-placing; pneuma douleias (G1397), the spirit of bondage; summartureo (G4828), to bear witness jointly; Aramaic Abba (G5), Father.
roots_lines: Greek huiothesia (G5206) — adoption; Romans 8:15, 8:23, 9:4, Galatians 4:5, Ephesians 1:5 — all five occurrences, all Paul.
Greek summarturei (G4828) — beareth witness with; Romans 8:16, 2:15, 9:1.
Aramaic Abba (G5) — father; Romans 8:15, Galatians 4:6, Mark 14:36.
usage: “Not… the spirit of bondage again to fear” — the diagnosis.
“Whereby we cry, Abba, Father” — what the witness sounds like.
“Waiting for the adoption” — adopted, and still waiting.

pos: n. phrase (the Lord's own title for the Holy Spirit in the upper room, given three times, each with a different work attached)
etymology: Greek to pneuma tes aletheias. The title occurs four times in John's writings and nowhere else in the New Testament; it is the Comforter's name when His relation to truth is in view.
biblical_def: The Spirit of truth is named three times in the farewell discourse. First, as one the world cannot have: “the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him” (John 14:17). Second, as a witness to Christ: “the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me” (John 15:26). Third, as a guide who does not speak of Himself: “when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself… He shall glorify me” (John 16:13–14). John's letter makes the title a test: “Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error” (1Jn 4:6). And the Lord had already joined the two words at a well: “they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth” (John 4:24).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines truth as conformity to fact or reality, exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be; and, in Scripture, the true doctrine of the gospel, and the Holy Spirit as the Spirit of truth who guides into all truth.
webster_full: TRUTH, n. Conformity to fact or reality; exact accordance with that which is, or has been, or shall be.
2. True state of facts or things.
3. Conformity of words to thoughts, which is called moral truth.
4. Veracity; purity from falsehood; practice of speaking truth; habitual disposition to speak truth.
5. Correct opinion.
6. Fidelity; constancy.
Sanctify them through thy truth; thy word is truth. John 17.
scriptures: John 14:17
Even the Spirit of truth; whom the world cannot receive, because it seeth him not, neither knoweth him: but ye know him; for he dwelleth with you, and shall be in you.
John 15:26
But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
John 16:13

Howbeit when he, the Spirit of truth, is come, he will guide you into all truth: for he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak: and he will shew you things to come.
We are of God: he that knoweth God heareth us; he that is not of God heareth not us. Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error.
John 4:24
God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
corruption_summary: The Spirit's guidance is claimed for private impressions, and every promise in the upper room ties Him to Christ's words and to the apostles who would write them.
corruption_paragraphs: John 16:13 is the most quoted and most misapplied of the three. He will guide you into all truth is taken as a general promise to every believer of direct, ongoing revelation, and the surrounding clauses are dropped. The promise is made to the eleven in the upper room; it is fulfilled first in their teaching and writing, which is why the church has a New Testament at all; and the Spirit's method is specified in the same sentence — he shall not speak of himself; but whatsoever he shall hear, that shall he speak. A Spirit who does not speak of Himself is not the author of impressions that cannot be checked against what He already said.

The Reformed have therefore tied the Spirit's guidance to the Word without apology, and the upper room supports them. John 14:26 says He will bring to remembrance all things that I have said unto you; 15:26 says He will testify of me; 16:14 says He shall glorify me, receiving of mine and shewing it unto you. Three times the content of His work is Christ. A claimed leading of the Spirit that draws attention to the person led, or that contradicts or supplements what Christ said, fails the test the Lord Himself set for identifying the Spirit of truth.

First John 4:6 turns the title into an instrument and its criterion is startlingly plain: he that knoweth God heareth us — the apostles — hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error. Apostolic doctrine is the touchstone, which for a later generation means the apostolic writings. That is not a lower view of the Spirit; it is the view He gave of Himself. John 4:24 keeps the balance from tipping into mere correctness: worship is in spirit and in truth, and the Samaritan woman was corrected on both counts in a single conversation.
roots_summary: Greek pneuma tes aletheias (G4151, G225), the Spirit of truth; parakletos (G3875), Comforter, advocate; hodegeo (G3594), to guide, lead the way; pneuma tes planes (G4106), the spirit of error.
roots_lines: Greek to pneuma tes aletheias (G225) — the Spirit of truth; John 14:17, 15:26, 16:13, 1 John 4:6 — all four occurrences.
Greek hodegesei (G3594) — he will guide; John 16:13, and of the blind leading the blind, Matthew 15:14.
Greek pneuma tes planes (G4106) — spirit of error, of wandering; 1 John 4:6 only.
usage: “He shall not speak of himself” — the Spirit's own method, in the promise.
“He shall testify of me” — the content of His work is Christ.
“Hereby know we the spirit of truth, and the spirit of error” — a touchstone.

pos: n. phrase (holding one's ground under pressure; the posture Paul commands at the end of the armour passage and throughout his letters)
etymology: Greek steko, to stand fast, a late form built from the perfect of histemi, to stand — literally, to have taken one's stand and to be still standing there. It is a military word before it is a moral one.
biblical_def: Standing firm is the goal of the whole armour: “that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand. Stand therefore” (Eph 6:13–14). Paul gives it in four commands to Corinth: “Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong” (1Co 16:13). He gives it a specific ground at Galatia: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage” (Gal 5:1). He makes it corporate at Philippi: “that ye stand fast in one spirit, with one mind striving together for the faith of the gospel” (Php 1:27). And he warns the confident: “let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall” (1Co 10:12).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stand as to be upon the feet, as an animal; to remain firm, to be fixed or steady, not to vacillate; and, to stand fast, to be fixed, to be unshaken or immovable.
webster_full: STAND, v.i. To be upon the feet, as an animal; not to sit, kneel or lie.
2. To be erect, supported by the roots, as a tree or other plant.
3. To remain firm; to be fixed or steady; not to vacillate.
4. To be placed with regard to order or rank.
To stand fast, to be fixed; to be unshaken or immovable.
STEADFAST, a. Fast fixed; firm; firmly fixed or established; as the steadfast globe of earth.
scriptures: Eph 6:13
Wherefore take unto you the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to withstand in the evil day, and having done all, to stand.
Eph 6:14
Stand therefore, having your loins girt about with truth, and having on the breastplate of righteousness;
Watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong.
Gal 5:1
Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage.
Wherefore let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall.
corruption_summary: Standing is confused with advancing or with stubbornness, and Ephesians 6 describes a man holding a position he did not capture.
corruption_paragraphs: The armour passage is often preached as an assault, and its verbs are all defensive. Four times in three verses the word is stand — stand against the wiles, withstand in the evil day, having done all, to stand; stand therefore — and the pieces of armour are shield, helmet, breastplate, with one weapon, which is the word. The position was won by someone else. Ephesians 1 and 2 have already said that the believer is seated with Christ in heavenly places; chapter 6 tells him to hold ground that is already his, against a pressure whose aim is to move him off it. That is the shape of Christian resistance, and it is humbler than a charge.

First Corinthians 10:12 is the guard against the other error, which is to mistake obstinacy for firmness. Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall — spoken about Israel in the wilderness, who had every sacrament and fell anyway. The men most confident that they are standing are the ones Paul warns, and the confidence is itself the symptom. Standing firm in Scripture is never self-assured; the same passage that commands it lists what the believer stands in — the faith, the liberty, one spirit — and none of those is himself.

Galatians 5:1 shows what is at stake and it is specific. Stand fast in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. The Galatians were not being pushed toward vice; they were being drawn back toward a religion of law that felt safer, and Paul treats the drift as a fall. The pressure a believer must stand against is as often respectable as it is wicked, and Philippians 1:27 adds that the standing is done shoulder to shoulder — in one spirit, with one mind — because a man alone in a line does not hold it long.
roots_summary: Greek steko (G4739), to stand fast; histemi (G2476), to stand, set; anthistemi (G436), to withstand, resist; andrizomai (G407), to act like a man.
roots_lines: Greek steko (G4739) — to stand fast; 1 Corinthians 16:13, Galatians 5:1, Philippians 1:27, 4:1, 1 Thessalonians 3:8.
Greek anthistemi (G436) — to withstand, resist; Ephesians 6:13, James 4:7, 1 Peter 5:9.
Greek andrizesthe (G407) — quit you like men, be manly; 1 Corinthians 16:13 only.
usage: “Having done all, to stand” — a position held, not captured.
“Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed” — the confidence is the symptom.
“Be not entangled again” — the pressure was respectable.

pos: n. phrase (the joy of the LORD as a source of strength — Nehemiah's word to a weeping congregation)
etymology: Hebrew chedvah, gladness, a rare word used twice in the Old Testament, and maoz, a stronghold or place of safety — so that Nehemiah's phrase reads almost literally, the gladness of the LORD is your fortress.
biblical_def: The strength of joy is Nehemiah's instruction to a people weeping at the reading of the Law: “neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength” (Neh 8:10). David gives the sequence: “The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth” (Psa 28:7). Habakkuk gives it in a famine: “Although the fig tree shall not blossom… Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation” (Hab 3:17–18). Its source is a Presence: “in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore” (Psa 16:11). And it is commanded from a prison: “Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice” (Php 4:4).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines joy as the passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; gladness, exultation, exhilaration of spirits; and strength as that property of an animal body by which it is enabled to move itself or other bodies, and, figuratively, firmness, security.
webster_full: JOY, n. The passion or emotion excited by the acquisition or expectation of good; that excitement of pleasurable feelings which is caused by success, good fortune, the gratification of desire or some good possessed; gladness; exultation; exhilaration of spirits.
2. Gayety; mirth; festivity.
3. Happiness; felicity.
STRENGTH, n. That property or quality of an animal body by which it is enabled to move itself or other bodies.
4. Firmness; solidity or toughness; the quality of bodies by which they sustain the application of force without breaking or yielding.
10. Support; that which supports; security.
scriptures: Neh 8:10

Then he said unto them, Go your way, eat the fat, and drink the sweet, and send portions unto them for whom nothing is prepared: for this day is holy unto our Lord: neither be ye sorry; for the joy of the LORD is your strength.
Psa 28:7
The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth; and with my song will I praise him.
Hab 3:18
Yet I will rejoice in the LORD, I will joy in the God of my salvation.
Thou wilt shew me the path of life: in thy presence is fulness of joy; at thy right hand there are pleasures for evermore.
Php 4:4
Rejoice in the Lord alway: and again I say, Rejoice.
corruption_summary: Joy is expected to be produced by the believer and then used as fuel, and every text puts the joy on God's side of the sentence.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 8:10 is quoted as a motivational maxim and it is a pastoral intervention. The people were weeping because the Law had been read to them and understood, and the weeping was appropriate; Nehemiah, Ezra and the Levites tell them to stop, to go and eat the fat and drink the sweet and send portions to those who have nothing prepared, because the day is holy. The joy is of the LORD — His joy, the gladness that belongs to Him and is His to give — and it is a stronghold, a place to retreat into. A congregation told to be joyful as a duty has been handed the burden; the verse hands them the fortress.

Psalm 28:7 gives the sequence in the right order and it is easily reversed. The LORD is my strength and my shield; my heart trusted in him, and I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth. Trust, then help, then joy — the joy is the consequence of having been helped, not the precondition of it. Believers who try to generate the joy first, in order to qualify for the help, are running the psalm backwards, and Psalm 16:11 locates the supply in a place rather than a technique: in thy presence is fulness of joy.

Habakkuk 3:17–18 is the proof that this joy is not prosperity in a religious costume. The fig tree does not blossom, there is no fruit in the vines, the olive fails, the fields yield no meat, the flock is cut off and there is no herd in the stalls — a complete agricultural collapse, itemised — yet I will rejoice in the LORD. The joy survives the loss of every ordinary reason for it because its object was never those reasons. Paul commands the same thing from a Roman prison with a capital charge pending, and repeats it, because he knew it would be resisted.
roots_summary: Hebrew chedvah (H2304), gladness, joy; maoz (H4581), stronghold, strength; alaz (H5937), to exult, rejoice; Greek chairo (G5463), to rejoice.
roots_lines: Hebrew chedvath YHWH hi ma'uzzekem (H2304, H4581) — the joy of the LORD is your strength, your stronghold; Nehemiah 8:10; chedvah also 1 Chronicles 16:27.
Hebrew alaz (H5937) — to exult; Habakkuk 3:18, Psalm 28:7, 68:4.
Hebrew soba semachot (H7648, H8057) — fulness of joy; Psalm 16:11.
usage: “The joy of the LORD is your strength” — His joy, and a stronghold.
“I am helped: therefore my heart greatly rejoiceth” — the order matters.
“Although the fig tree shall not blossom… yet I will rejoice” — joy with every ordinary reason removed.

pos: n. phrase (that over which a man trips — an obstacle to faith or to a brother's conscience; the AV writes it as one word)
etymology: Greek skandalon, the trigger-stick of a trap, then the trap itself, then anything that trips; and proskomma, a thing struck against. The AV's stumblingblock renders both, and English scandal descends from the first.
biblical_def: A stumbling block is what a man falls over, and Scripture applies the figure to two very different things. Christ Himself is one to unbelief: “we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness” (1Co 1:23); “Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed” (Rom 9:33); “a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient” (1Pe 2:8). The other kind a believer is forbidden to be: “judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way” (Rom 14:13). The Law had forbidden the literal version: “Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind” (Lev 19:14).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines stumbling-block as any cause of stumbling; that which causes to err; and, in Scripture, an obstacle to faith, or an occasion of sin.
webster_full: STUMBLING-BLOCK, STUMBLING-STONE, n. Any cause of stumbling; that which causes to err.
We preach Christ crucified, to the Jews a stumbling-block. 1 Cor. 1.
Let us not put a stumbling-block or an occasion to fall in his brother's way. Rom. 14.
OFFENSE, n. In Scripture, a stumbling-block; a cause of falling or of sin.
scriptures: But we preach Christ crucified, unto the Jews a stumblingblock, and unto the Greeks foolishness;
Rom 9:33
As it is written, Behold, I lay in Sion a stumblingstone and rock of offence: and whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed.
And a stone of stumbling, and a rock of offence, even to them which stumble at the word, being disobedient: whereunto also they were appointed.
Let us not therefore judge one another any more: but judge this rather, that no man put a stumblingblock or an occasion to fall in his brother's way.
Thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind, but shalt fear thy God: I am the LORD.
corruption_summary: The two stumbling blocks are confused, so that the church removes the offence of the cross and keeps the offences it causes its brethren.
corruption_paragraphs: First Corinthians 1:23 names a stumbling block that must not be removed. Christ crucified offended the Jews because a crucified man was accursed by the Law, and offended the Greeks because a dying god was absurd, and Paul preached it anyway and refused to plane the edges off. Romans 9:33 says God laid the stone in Sion — the offence is His placement, and the same verse promises that whosoever believeth on him shall not be ashamed. A gospel adjusted until nobody trips over it has had its stone quietly taken up, and there is then nothing left to stand on either.

Romans 14 names the stumbling block that must be removed, and it is the believer himself. The chapter is about meat and days, and Paul's ruling is that the strong Christian, who is right about the meat, may nonetheless be sinning by eating it in front of a brother whose conscience cannot bear it. The offence there is not the truth but the liberty exercised without love, and verse 15 puts the weight on it: destroy not him with thy meat, for whom Christ died. The church tends to get these exactly backwards — softening the cross for the world's comfort and asserting its freedoms at its brethren's expense.

Leviticus 19:14 is the root and it is about cruelty rather than doctrine: thou shalt not curse the deaf, nor put a stumblingblock before the blind. Both are sins the victim cannot detect — the deaf man does not hear the curse, the blind man does not see the block — and the verse ends but shalt fear thy God, because He sees both. That is the principle underneath Romans 14. The stumbling block a Christian lays for a weaker brother is usually one the brother cannot see coming and the layer can, and the fear of God is what should stop his hand.
roots_summary: Greek skandalon (G4625), a snare, stumbling block, offence; proskomma (G4348), a stumbling, obstacle; lithos proskommatos (G3037), stone of stumbling; Hebrew mikshol (H4383), a stumbling block, obstacle.
roots_lines: Greek skandalon (G4625) — stumbling block, offence, the trigger of a trap; 1 Corinthians 1:23, Romans 9:33, 14:13, Matthew 18:7, Galatians 5:11.
Greek proskomma (G4348) — an obstacle struck against; Romans 9:32–33, 14:13, 14:20, 1 Peter 2:8.
Hebrew mikshol (H4383) — stumbling block; Leviticus 19:14, Isaiah 57:14, Ezekiel 3:20, 14:3.
usage: “Unto the Jews a stumblingblock” — and Paul preached it anyway.
“No man put a stumblingblock… in his brother's way” — the one to remove.
“Nor put a stumblingblock before the blind… but shalt fear thy God” — He sees the block.

pos: n. phrase (the Lord's answer to Paul's thorn: grace enough for the affliction, with the affliction left in place)
etymology: Greek arkei soi he charis mou — my grace suffices for thee. The verb arkeo means to be enough, to ward off want; it is the word behind content in Hebrews 13:5 and the root of the English autarky.
biblical_def: Sufficient grace is the Lord's reply to a prayer He declined: “there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me… For this thing I besought the Lord thrice, that it might depart from me. And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness” (2Co 12:7–9). Paul's response reorganises his whole valuation: “Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me… for when I am weak, then am I strong” (2Co 12:9–10). The same sufficiency is promised for giving: “God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work” (2Co 9:8). And Hebrews sets the time: “grace to help in time of need” (Heb 4:16).
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines sufficient as enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; competent; and grace as the free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from Him, and the divine influence that renews the heart and sustains the believer.
webster_full: SUFFICIENT, a. Enough; equal to the end proposed; adequate to wants; competent; as provision sufficient for the family.
My grace is sufficient for thee. 2 Cor. 12.
GRACE, n. Favor; good will; kindness; disposition to oblige another.
2. Appropriately, the free unmerited love and favor of God, the spring and source of all the benefits men receive from him.
3. Favorable influence of God; divine influence or the influence of the spirit, in renewing the heart and restraining from sin.
scriptures: And lest I should be exalted above measure through the abundance of the revelations, there was given to me a thorn in the flesh, the messenger of Satan to buffet me, lest I should be exalted above measure.

And he said unto me, My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness. Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.
Therefore I take pleasure in infirmities, in reproaches, in necessities, in persecutions, in distresses for Christ's sake: for when I am weak, then am I strong.
And God is able to make all grace abound toward you; that ye, always having all sufficiency in all things, may abound to every good work:
Heb 4:16
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need.
corruption_summary: The thorn is treated as the problem and grace as the solution that should remove it, and the text records the thorn staying.
corruption_paragraphs: The passage is more uncomfortable than its famous sentence. Paul had a thorn — he never says what — and calls it a messenger of Satan sent to buffet him, and prays three times for it to go, and it does not go. What he receives instead is a sentence, and the sentence is the whole doctrine: my grace is sufficient for thee. Not my grace will remove it. Any account of sufficient grace that expects the thorn to be withdrawn as evidence of the grace has reversed the passage; the grace was proved by the thorn remaining and Paul continuing.

The reason given is the part that offends the modern instinct most: my strength is made perfect in weakness. Perfected, completed, brought to its full working — in the exact place where the man has run out. Paul's response is not resignation but a reorganised accounting, and its verbs are startling: most gladly will I rather glory in my infirmities, I take pleasure in infirmities, reproaches, necessities, persecutions, distresses. He is not pretending they do not hurt; he has discovered what they are for. The thorn was given, he says — twice — lest I should be exalted above measure, after being caught up to the third heaven. The affliction was the antidote to the revelation.

Hebrews 4:16 supplies the timing and it is the practical half of the doctrine: grace to help in time of need. The sufficiency is not a reservoir issued in advance so that a man can inspect it and feel secure; it is delivered at the point of need, in the quantity the need requires, and not before. That is why the anxious question — could I bear it if that happened? — has no answer now and is not meant to. The grace for a trial is issued with the trial. Second Corinthians 9:8 extends the same principle to money, and its piling of all is deliberate: all grace, always, all sufficiency, all things, every good work.

roots_lines: Greek arkei soi (G714) — is sufficient for thee; 2 Corinthians 12:9, and arkeo of contentment, Hebrews 13:5, 1 Timothy 6:8.
Greek skolops te sarki (G4647) — a thorn in the flesh; 2 Corinthians 12:7 only.
Greek pasan autarkeian (G841) — all sufficiency; 2 Corinthians 9:8, 1 Timothy 6:6.
usage: “I besought the Lord thrice” — and the thorn stayed.
“My strength is made perfect in weakness” — completed, where the man ran out.
“Grace to help in time of need” — issued with the trial, not before.
